hookLine: She was handed a number and told to bide her time. Forty-seven. Two hours later, she got up and left.

OP.secondary: United States Court of Appeals, First Circuit — 31 October 1995

OP.label: Awarded by the jury. Not reduced by a dollar.

ACT_1.secondary: Sixty-five. A widow. Inside the emergency room no later than one o'clock.

items.label: Angel Correa: he implored the receptionist, she has chest pains
The Hospital: its personnel were told only dizzy and nauseated

ACT_1.quote: the thicket of conflicting testimony and the chasmal gaps in the direct evidence
ACT_1.attribution: Judge Bruce Selya, Correa v. Hospital San Francisco, 69 F.3d 1184 (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_1.label: The number a Hospital employee assigned her, before telling her to bide her time

ACT_1.secondary: Her plan allowed any appropriate provider in an emergency. She was entitled to be there.

ACT_1.label: The number called as her son left, an hour in

ACT_1.quote: The Hospital staff continued blithely to ignore her.
ACT_1.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_1.label: Physicians who saw her in that time

ACT_1.primary: SHE LEFT BECAUSE SHE HAD BEEN WAITING
ACT_1.secondary: The opinion does not describe anyone turning her away. It does not describe anyone discharging her.
Blood pressure ninety over sixty. Intravenous fluids. Medicine to control the vomiting.

events.text: Inside the emergency room, at the latest
She gets up and drives to a clinic
She dies there, under a physician's care

ACT_1.primary: AT ANOTHER FACILITY, UNDER A PHYSICIAN'S CARE
ACT_1.secondary: The opinion never says the delay killed her, and never says she would have lived
A nurse called Hospmed to say the patient would be coming. Dr. Rojas's recollection.

lines: NOT WHETHER SHE WAS TREATED WELL.

ACT_2.secondary: An emergency condition. No appropriate screening. An improper transfer.
Footnote seven. The court of appeals never reviewed it, and it plays no part in what this case decided.

items.label: On the decedent's own account, payable to the heirs
The survivors' pain, suffering and mental anguish

ACT_2.quote: the trial judge's unconditional seal of approval
ACT_2.attribution: Correa (1st Cir. 1995), n.10, on the district court's treatment of the award

ACT_2.label: Assignments of error on appeal. None of them worked.

ACT_2.quote: This appeal requires us to interpret, for the first time, the Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act
ACT_2.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco (1st Cir. 1995), opening line

ACT_2.quote: about the increasing number of reports that hospital emergency rooms are refusing to accept or treat patients with emergency conditions if the patient does not have medical insurance
ACT_2.attribution: H.R. Rep. No. 241(I), 99th Cong., 1st Sess. 27 (1986), quoted in Correa (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_2.secondary: An appropriate screening — and stabilisation if an emergency condition is found

ACT_2.label: The ceiling on the penalty for each negligent violation

ACT_2.secondary: No appropriate screening — or bade farewell without stabilising. This case went through the first.

ACT_2.quote: This suggestion finds no purchase in the statute's text, and we reject it.
ACT_2.attribution: Correa (1st Cir. 1995), n.5, rejecting the contrary dictum

ACT_2.primary: BUT THE DAMAGES REMEDY STILL REQUIRES HARM
ACT_2.secondary: Civil penalties are imposable irrespective of resulting harm. The statutory damage remedy is not.

ACT_3.primary: IT HAD WRITTEN A MANUAL ON EMTALA COMPLIANCE
ACT_3.secondary: Its own executive told the jury he had trained the staff on it. Then it argued the law did not apply.

ACT_3.quote: This argument has the shrill ring of desperation.
ACT_3.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_3.label: Of American hospitals covered by EMTALA — the court's figure, given without a citation. Ninety-nine is not one hundred.

ACT_3.secondary: That she had no emergency condition when she reported to the facility — "doubly flawed"

ACT_3.quote: Credibility choices are generally for the jury, not for the court of appeals.
ACT_3.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_3.secondary: Nausea and dizziness might well herald the onset of an emergency condition — as Dr. Rojas explained

ACT_3.quote: Appropriate is one of the most wonderful weasel words in the dictionary
ACT_3.attribution: Cleland v. Bronson Health Care Group (6th Cir. 1990), quoted in Correa (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_3.quote: appropriateness, like nature, is a mutable cloud which is always and never the same
ACT_3.attribution: Judge Bruce Selya, after Emerson, in Correa (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_3.primary: THE TEST THE COURTS HAD BUILT
ACT_3.secondary: A screening reasonably calculated to identify critical conditions — provided uniformly to substantially similar complaints

items.label: A hospital that examines you badly has not broken this law
A hospital that examines you differently, or not at all, has

lines: REFER TO A PHYSICIAN AT ONCE.

ACT_3.quote: the Hospital's utter inability to produce any records
ACT_3.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_3.label: Records produced for a patient who had been inside for two hours

ACT_3.quote: we need not decide whether mere negligence in failing to expedite screening would itself violate the federal statute
ACT_3.attribution: Correa (1st Cir. 1995) — the door the panel left shut

ACT_4.quote: facts at trial, as in life, do not always appear in black and white
ACT_4.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_4.label: People shown to have refused her, discharged her, or told her to leave

ACT_4.quote: it gave the patient a number, and would have ministered to her had she waited
ACT_4.attribution: Correa (1st Cir. 1995) — the Court's statement of the Hospital's point

ACT_4.primary: THE FIRST REASON · THE TELEPHONE CALL
ACT_4.secondary: Described by Dr. Rojas — and the panel notes, as an aside, that HSF called her as its witness

ACT_4.quote: was itself responsible for truncating her wait
ACT_4.attribution: Correa (1st Cir. 1995), on what the jury could have found if it believed the physician

ACT_4.quote: regardless of motive, a complete failure to attend a patient who presents a condition that practically everyone knows may indicate an immediate and acute threat to life can constitute a denial of an appropriate medical screening examination
ACT_4.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco, 69 F.3d 1184 (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_4.quote: EMTALA should be read to proscribe both actual and constructive dumping of patients.
ACT_4.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco, 69 F.3d 1184 (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_4.quote: a high number and a cold shoulder
ACT_4.attribution: Correa (1st Cir. 1995), on what the jury could have concluded she received

ACT_4.secondary: That liability requires an economic motive. She was insured, so none could have existed.

ACT_4.quote: covers all patients who come to a hospital's emergency department, and requires that they be appropriately screened, regardless of insurance status or ability to pay
ACT_4.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco (1st Cir. 1995), the holding on motive

ACT_4.secondary: All insurance plans are not created equal — the panel's footnote on why insurance does not end the inquiry

ACT_4.quote: A participating hospital may not delay provision of an appropriate medical screening examination required under subsection (a) of this section … in order to inquire about the individual's method of payment or insurance status.
ACT_4.attribution: 42 U.S.C. § 1395dd(h), reproduced in the appendix to Correa (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_5.secondary: That EMTALA pays the patient's harm, and not seven relatives' grief. The court never decided it.

events.text: Signed by all counsel. No mention of it.
Three legal issues. Not this one.

ACT_5.quote: Based on this somber record of inattention
ACT_5.attribution: Correa (1st Cir. 1995), on the defence the hospital forfeited

ACT_5.quote: a classic example of a litigant locking the barn door long after the horse has bolted
ACT_5.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_5.secondary: A renewed motion cannot introduce a theory not distinctly articulated at the close of the evidence

ACT_5.quote: grossly excessive, inordinate, shocking to the conscience of the court, or so high that it would be a denial of justice to permit it to stand
ACT_5.attribution: Segal v. Gilbert Color Sys. (1st Cir. 1984), quoting Grunenthal (1968) — the excessiveness standard applied in Correa

ACT_5.primary: THE HUB OF THE FAMILY CIRCLE
ACT_5.secondary: A matriarchal figure. Her son lived with her; her two daughters resided nearby.

ACT_5.label: Months between the grandchildren losing their father and losing her
Up to five years, an expert said, for the grandchildren's suffering to abate

ACT_5.primary: THE TRUNK OF THE FAMILY TREE
ACT_5.secondary: One witness's description of her. The sums awarded do not shock the court's collective conscience.

ACT_5.quote: Though generous, the jury's assessment does not outstrip the bounds of reason.
ACT_5.attribution: Correa v. Hospital San Francisco (1st Cir. 1995)

ACT_5.quote: Ms. Gonzalez spent the few remaining hours of her life in agony, beset by nausea, dizziness, and chest pains
ACT_5.attribution: Correa (1st Cir. 1995), giving its reason for the award on her own account

ENDING.secondary: A jury found a screening violation. The court held that finding unimpugnable, and said the statute reaches constructive dumping.

ENDING.primary: IT DOES NOT HOLD THAT THE TRANSFER WAS UNLAWFUL
IT DID NOT CALL A MEDICAL EXPERT
ENDING.secondary: It asked what the hospital's own rules required, and then what the hospital could produce.

items.label: Rules of its own that the opinion lists
Sheets of paper it could produce for her

ENDING.primary: THERE IS NO VILLAIN IN THIS RECORD
ENDING.secondary: No decision was ever testified to. That is what the court's word is for. Constructive.

_notes.script: episodes/_planning/EP63_correa_script.en.v002.md is the confirmed script. It was CUT on 2026-08-06 after the real narration master measured over the ceiling; do not restore anything from an earlier revision.
_notes.runtime: MEASURED, not modelled: the ffprobed ElevenLabs master gives 1898.6s for 5121 narration words, inside the contract band [1620,1920]. The scripts' own 176 words-per-finished-minute model runs 8-10 percent optimistic and is what put two films on this slate over the ceiling. Re-ffprobe after any script edit and check against 1920 before committing anything downstream.
